name: Bathsheba
bio:
Bathsheba was the daughter of Eliam, who was himself the son of David's counselor-turned-conspirator Ahithophel the Gilonite, making Bathsheba Ahithophel's granddaughter (2 Samuel 23:34). She was the wife of Uriah the Hittite, whom David saw bathing from his rooftop while her husband was away at war. David sent for her, and though Scripture gives her no recorded words of consent or objection, he lay with her; when she sent word that she was pregnant, David's attempt to cover the matter by recalling Uriah from the battlefield failed, and he ultimately arranged for Uriah's death in battle. After a period of mourning for her husband, Bathsheba was brought to David's house and became his wife, bearing him a son — but "the thing David had done displeased the LORD" (2 Samuel 11:2-5, 26-27).

The prophet Nathan's parable and confrontation that followed exposed the full weight of what had happened to her and to Uriah, and the son born of that union died in infancy as part of the LORD's judgment, despite David's anguished fasting and prayer (2 Samuel 12:1-23). David then comforted Bathsheba, and she bore another son, whom David named Solomon; the LORD loved him and sent word through Nathan that he should be called Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:24-25). ## 📖 Core Story: Securing Solomon's Throne

As David lay old and dying, his son Adonijah declared himself king without David's knowledge. The prophet Nathan came to Bathsheba and warned her that she and Solomon would be in mortal danger if Adonijah's bid succeeded, and coached her to go remind David of his earlier oath that Solomon would reign after him. Bathsheba went in to David and did exactly that, and while she was still speaking, Nathan arrived and confirmed her account; moved, David swore on the spot that Solomon would be made king that very day, and Bathsheba bowed before him in gratitude (1 Kings 1:11-31). Solomon was anointed king at Gihon that same day, decisively ending Adonijah's attempt.

After David's death, Adonijah came to Bathsheba and asked her to request that Solomon give him Abishag, the young woman who had attended David in his old age, as his wife. Bathsheba, apparently not recognizing the danger in the request, brought it to Solomon, who received his mother with great honor, seating her at his right hand — but read Adonijah's request as a fresh bid for the throne itself, and had him executed that same day (1 Kings 2:13-25).
